# `httpd`

An HTTP/1.1 server written in Colibri on top of `net`: a router, request bodies, streamed responses, limits and timeouts, and a graceful stop.

```colibri
import httpd
```

Needs the `net` and `os` capabilities.

Back to the [standard library index](README.md).

## Types

### `Handler`

```text
type Handler = fn(Request) -> Result[Response]
```

A function that answers a request. An `err` becomes an error response: a `Failure` (see
`fail`) gives its status, any other error gives 500.

### `Options`

```text
struct Options {
    max_request_line: int = 8192
    max_header_bytes: int = 65536
    max_headers: int = 100
    max_body_bytes: int = 10485760
    header_timeout: float = 10.0
    idle_timeout: float = 60.0
    body_timeout: float = 30.0
    write_timeout: float = 30.0
    handler_timeout: float = 60.0
    max_connections: int = 1024
    server_name: str = ""
    log_errors: bool = true
}
```

The limits and timeouts of a server. A timeout is in seconds, and a limit in bytes unless it
says otherwise. `listen` is given one and refuses a negative limit, and a line limit outside 1 to 1 GiB.

- `max_request_line`: The request line without its line end. A longer line is answered with 414.
- `max_header_bytes`: All the field lines (and trailer lines) of one request, each with its CRLF. More is 431.
- `max_headers`: The field lines of one request. More is 431.
- `max_body_bytes`: The bytes of a body a handler may read; `Request.set_body_limit` changes it for one request. For a chunked body the total counts the data and also the bytes of the size lines after their hex digits (whitespace and chunk extensions), so that many small chunks with large extensions cannot make the server read without bound; a total over the limit is 413. A handler that calls `Request.body` holds up to this many bytes for each such request.
- `header_timeout`: The whole head of a request: its fields have this long from the end of the request line, and on a new connection the empty lines and the request line have this long from the accept. No sequence of bytes extends a deadline.
- `idle_timeout`: How long a kept-alive connection may wait for its next request: one deadline for the empty lines and the request line together (the server cannot tell when the first byte of a request arrived, so `header_timeout` starts only after the request line).
- `body_timeout`: Each read of a body piece (at most 64 KiB, or what is left of the body, or the `max` a handler gave `Request.read`) must deliver the whole piece within this time. A client that sends a byte at a time does not extend it.
- `write_timeout`: Each write of a response (a piece of at most 256 KiB).
- `handler_timeout`: From the call of the handler to its `Response`; 0 is none. A handler that is out of time is cancelled (its `defer`s run, up to the first point where one would wait: the runtime abandons a `defer` that suspends while its coroutine is being cancelled, so a cleanup that does I/O is cut there) and the client gets `503 Service Unavailable` with `Connection: close`; the event is logged. A sweeper looks at most every quarter of a second while some handler runs, so the precision is that, and a server with no handler running has nothing on a timer. A handler that computes without ever suspending cannot be bounded: nothing else runs while it does. A panic of the handler (or of the closure of a stream) is contained: 500 and a close, or a cut stream, and a log line. A coroutine that a handler starts and never joins is not covered: its panic still ends `serve` and the program, as does the budget panic of a host that sets an instruction budget (it always reaches the host). The closure of a streamed response is not counted (a stream may be long): each of its writes has `write_timeout`, and it ends at `stop` after the grace period.
- `max_connections`: Open connections. At the cap the server stops accepting until one ends. What a connection costs (measured with the defaults): in a release build an idle one takes about 46 to 48 KiB, so a server holds about 16 MiB with none, about 61 MiB with 1,000 and about 490 MiB with 10,000. A debug build takes more: about 100 KiB for an idle one (measured before a connection got its own child coroutine, so a little more today), about 107 KiB with a request line of 8,000 bytes pending, and about 143 KiB at worst, with fields kept up to `max_header_bytes` and a field line of that size pending; plus 64 KiB while it lingers or drains. A handler that calls `Request.body` or `Request.text` holds up to `max_body_bytes` more for its request (10 MiB by default), which is the application's choice: the server itself never holds a body. So the default 1,024 connections take about 16 MiB plus 46 to 48 MiB idle in a release build, and more with requests in flight or when handlers hold bodies.
- `server_name`: The `Server` header of every response; "" sends none.
- `log_errors`: Whether handler errors, panics and timeouts are written to stderr.

### `Failure`

```text
struct Failure {
    status: int
    message: str
}
```

An error with an HTTP status. A handler returns `err(httpd.fail(404, "no item 7"))` and the
client gets 404 with `message` as the body.

Implements `Show`, `IntoError`.

### `Headers`

```text
class Headers {
    // and private fields
```

The header fields of a request or a response. Names compare without regard to case. A name
can have several lines (`Set-Cookie`); `get` joins them with `, `, `get_all` keeps them apart.

### `BodyWriter`

```text
class BodyWriter {
    // and private fields
}
```

Where a streamed body is written. A connection gives one to the closure of `stream`.

#### `BodyWriter.write`

```text
fn write(self, data: Bytes) -> Result[()]
```

Writes `data`; empty data writes nothing. An `Err` means the peer is gone or too slow, or
the write went past the response's length, and the closure should pass it up with `?`. A
closure that writes again after an error is cancelled at that write: it stops there and
its `defer`s run, so a stream that ignores errors cannot spin.

#### `BodyWriter.write_str`

```text
fn write_str(self, text: str) -> Result[()]
```

### `Request`

```text
class Request {
    method: str
    target: str
    path: str
    query: str
    version: str
    headers: Headers
    remote_addr: str
    // and private fields
}
```

A request, as a handler sees it. A program cannot build one (it has fields of the module):
the server makes them, and `test_request` makes one for a test.

- `method`: As sent; methods are case-sensitive (RFC 9110 9.1).
- `target`: The request-target as sent: `/items/7?x=1`.
- `path`: The path, not decoded: `/items/7`, and `*` for `OPTIONS *`.
- `query`: What follows the `?`, not decoded; "" when there is none.
- `version`: `HTTP/1.1` or `HTTP/1.0`.
- `remote_addr`: The peer's `host:port`.

#### `Request.header`

```text
fn header(self, name: str) -> str?
```

A header field: every value of the name joined with `, `.

#### `Request.host`

```text
fn host(self) -> str
```

The host the request is addressed to: the authority of an absolute-form target, else the
`Host` field; "" in an HTTP/1.0 request that has neither.

#### `Request.param`

```text
fn param(self, name: str) -> str?
```

A parameter of the route that matched, percent-decoded: `:id` or `*rest` of the pattern.
The value is what the client wrote, decoded once: `%2F` gives a `/` inside the value, and
a program that uses it as a file name or a key must check it itself. A `.` or `..`
segment, and an escape of a control character, never reach a handler: the router answers
400 for them.

#### `Request.query_values`

```text
fn query_values(self) -> Map[str, List[str]]
```

All the parameters of the query, decoded; see `parse_query` for how. The query is already
bounded by `max_request_line`, so it is parsed whole, without a cap on its pairs.

#### `Request.query_value`

```text
fn query_value(self, name: str) -> str?
```

The first value of a parameter of the query, decoded.

#### `Request.content_length`

```text
fn content_length(self) -> int?
```

The length the body is declared to have: 0 when there is no body, `none` when it is
chunked.

#### `Request.set_body_limit`

```text
fn set_body_limit(self, bytes: int)
```

Replaces `max_body_bytes` for this request. Call it before the first read.

#### `Request.read`

```text
fn read(self, max: int) -> Result[Bytes]
```

The next piece of the body, 1 to `max` bytes, empty at the end. A body over the limit is a
413 `Failure`, a body that stops short a 400, a timeout a 408.

#### `Request.body`

```text
fn body(self) -> Result[Bytes]
```

The rest of the body, whole.

#### `Request.text`

```text
fn text(self) -> Result[str]
```

The rest of the body as UTF-8; text that is not is a 400 `Failure`.

### `Router`

```text
class Router {
    // and private fields
}
```

Sends a request to the handler of the first pattern that fits its method and path. Build one
with `Router()`, add routes with `get`, `post` and the others, and serve `router.handler()`.

A pattern is `/`-separated segments: a literal (`items`), `:name` (one non-empty segment,
decoded into `req.param(name)`) and a last `*name` (the rest of the path, one or more
segments joined with `/`, the last possibly empty: `/files/*rest` takes `/files/a/b` and
`/files/`, not `/files`). A literal beats `:name`, which beats `*name`, decided segment by
segment from the left and whatever the order of registration. There is no trailing-slash
redirect. A literal is compared with the segment as it came on the wire, so it matches what
`Request.path` says: `/admin` does not match `/%61dmin`. Only the values of `:name` and
`*name` are percent-decoded. A literal is written as it appears in a URL, so it may hold
`%XX` escapes and then matches exactly that text, byte for byte: `%2f` and `%2F` are two
different literals, and a client that writes the other one gets a 404. A pattern that is malformed, that has a
literal that is not valid path text (a space, a control character, `?`, `#`, a bad escape, a
`.` or `..`), that repeats a method and pattern, or that has a method that is not a token or
is a lower-case spelling of a standard method, panics where it is added.

The router answers by itself: 404 when no pattern fits the path, 405 with `Allow` when the
path fits under other methods, 501 for a method that is neither one of the standard methods
nor used by a route, 400 for a bad percent-escape in the path, for an escape of a control
character, and for a `.` or `..` segment (written with dots or `%2E`), which a proxy in front
resolves before it routes, HEAD by the route of GET when there is no route of HEAD (a route
of HEAD, even a `:name` one, comes first), and OPTIONS by 204 with `Allow` when there is no
route of OPTIONS.

#### `Router.handle`

```text
fn handle(self, method: str, pattern: str, handler: Handler)
```

Adds a route; panics when the pattern is malformed or the route exists.

#### `Router.get`

```text
fn get(self, pattern: str, handler: Handler)
```

#### `Router.post`

```text
fn post(self, pattern: str, handler: Handler)
```

#### `Router.put`

```text
fn put(self, pattern: str, handler: Handler)
```

### `Server`

```text
class Server {
    // and private fields
}
```

An HTTP server. `listen` makes one, `serve` runs it and `stop` ends it.

#### `Server.addr`

```text
fn addr(self) -> str
```

The address the server listens on, with the port the system picked.

#### `Server.connections`

```text
fn connections(self) -> int
```

The number of open connections.

#### `Server.serve`

```text
fn serve(self, handler: Handler) -> Result[()]
```

Accepts connections and answers their requests with `handler`, until `stop`; then it
returns `ok(())` once every connection has ended. An `err` if the server is already
serving or was stopped. It can be called on the main fiber or in a coroutine.

#### `Server.stop`

```text
fn stop(self, grace: float = 10.0)
```

Stops the server. It never suspends, so a handler may call it, and calling it twice is
fine. The listener is closed and idle connections are closed; a connection that is busy
finishes its response, which then says `Connection: close`. After `grace` seconds the
connections that are left are cancelled: their handlers and stream closures end, and
their `defer`s run up to the first point where one would wait (the runtime abandons a
`defer` that suspends while its coroutine is being cancelled).

## Functions

### `fail`

```text
fn fail(status: int, message: str) -> Error
```

The error `err(httpd.fail(status, message))` returns from a handler. A status outside 400 to
599 is answered as 500. `e.as[httpd.Failure]()` gives the `Failure` back.

```text
fn Headers() -> Headers
```


A response with no body: 204, 304, a bare 200.

```text

```

A `text/plain; charset=utf-8` response.

```text

```

### `bytes`

```text
fn bytes(
    status: int,
    body: Bytes,

) -> Response
```

A response with a body that is not text.

### `json`

```text
fn json[T](status: int, value: T) -> Result[Response]
```

An `application/json` response with the JSON of `value`; the error is the one `json.encode`
gives.

### `redirect`

```text
fn redirect(status: int, location: str) -> Response
```

A response with a `Location` header and no body (301, 302, 303, 307 or 308). The status is
not checked here: the server answers a status outside 200 to 599 with 500.

### `stream`

```text
fn stream(
    status: int,
    content_type: str,
    write: fn(BodyWriter) -> Result[()],
    length: int? = none,
) -> Response
```

A response whose body is written by `write` while it is sent: chunked when `length` is `none`,
and exactly `length` bytes otherwise. `write` runs in a coroutine of its own, and a panic or an
error of it ends the response where it is: the connection is closed without a last chunk, so
that a client sees a body that was cut. For an HTTP/1.0 request with no `length` the body
ends with the connection, so a stream that fails ends with an ordinary close, and the client
cannot tell that the body was cut (`net` has no way to reset a connection): give such a
stream a `length` if the client may be HTTP/1.0 and needs to know.

### `parse_query`

```text
fn parse_query(text: str, max_pairs: int = 1000) -> Result[Map[str, List[str]]]
```

The parameters of a query string (or of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body), each
name with all its values in the order they came. Names and values are decoded: `+` is a
space, a `%XX` escape is the byte, a bad escape stays as written, and bytes that are not UTF-8
become U+FFFD. A parameter with no `=` has the value "", and empty pairs (`a=1&&b=2`) are
skipped. More than `max_pairs` pairs is a 400 `Failure`: the work and the memory of a query
grow with its pairs, and a form handler should also lower `Request.set_body_limit` to what a
form of its own needs (the default allows 10 MiB).

### `test_request`

```text
fn test_request(
    method: str,
    target: str,
    headers: List[(str, str)] = [],
    body: Bytes = Bytes(),
    version: str = "HTTP/1.1",
    remote_addr: str = "127.0.0.1:0",
) -> Request
```

A request with an in-memory body and no connection, to test a handler: `test_request("POST",
"/items?x=1", [("Content-Type", "application/json")], body)`. The version is HTTP/1.1, and
the body limit is the default of `Options`; `version` can be `HTTP/1.0`, and `remote_addr` is
what `Request.remote_addr` says. A `Content-Length` is added when there is a body and no such
header is given, and one that is given and differs from the length of the body is a mistake of
the test and panics, like a `version` that is neither `HTTP/1.1` nor `HTTP/1.0`; a
`Transfer-Encoding` header is not acted on, the body is delivered as it is. A target that is
not a path or `*` is a mistake of the test and panics.

```text
fn Router() -> Router
```

### `listen`

```text
fn listen(addr: str, options: Options = Options {}) -> Result[Server]
```

Starts listening on `addr` (`host:port`; port 0 lets the system pick, and `server.addr()`
says which). The error is the `net` error (`AddrInUse` and the rest), or a message that names
the field of `options` that is not valid.

### `serve`

```text
fn serve(addr: str, handler: Handler, options: Options = Options {}) -> Result[()]
```

`listen` and then `serve`.
